 to submit an obituary
To share the story of your loved one, you can submit an obituary using any of the following methods: 
 Email : Please include the information from our Obituary Checklist (referenced below) to obits@pioneerpress.com .
 Online : Use our Self-Service Portal for a step-by-step guided process.
 Need assistance? Our obituary desk is here to help. Please call us at 651-228-5263 with any questions regarding the process or deadlines.
General Information:
 Your full name,
 Address (City, State, Zip Code),
 Phone number,
 And an alternate phone number (if any)
Obituary Specification:
 Name of Deceased,
 Obituary Text,
 A photo in a JPEG or PDF file is preferable, TIF and other files are accepted, we will contact you if there are any issues with the photo.
 Ad Run dates
 There is a discount for running more than one day, but this must be scheduled on the first run date to apply.
 If a photo is used, it must be used for both days for the discount to apply, contact us for more information.
Policies:
Verification of Death:
In order to publish obituaries a name and phone number of funeral home/cremation society is required. We must contact the funeral home/cremation society handling the arrangements during their business hours to verify the death. If the body of the deceased has been donated to the University of Minnesota Anatomy Bequest Program, or a similar program, their phone number is required for verification.
Please allow enough time to contact them especially during their limited weekend hours.
A death certificate is also acceptable for this purpose but only one of these two options are necessary.
Guestbook and Outside Websites:
We are not allowed to reference other media sources with a guestbook or an obituary placed elsewhere when placing an obituary in print and online. We may place a website for a funeral home or a family email for contact instead; contact us with any questions regarding this matter.
Obituary Process:
Once your submission is completed, we will fax or email a proof for review prior to publication in the newspaper. This proof includes price and days the notice is scheduled to appear.
 Please review the proof carefully. We must be notified of errors or changes before the notice appears in the Pioneer Press based on each day’s deadlines.
After publication, we will not be responsible for errors that may occur after final proofing.
Online:
Changes to an online obituary can be handled through the obituary desk. Call us with further questions.
Payment Procedure:
Pre-payment is required for all obituary notices prior to publication by the deadline specified below in our deadline schedule. Please call 651-228-5263 with your payment information after you have received the proof and approved its contents.
 Credit Card: Payment accepted by phone only due to PCI (Payment Card Industry) regulations
 EFT: Check by phone. Please provide your routing number and account number.
Rates:
 The minimum charge is $162 for the first 12 lines.
 Every line after the first 12 is $12.
 If the ad is under 12 lines it will be charged the minimum rate of $162.
 Obituaries including more than 40 lines will receive a 7.5% discount per line.
 On a second run date, receive a 20% discount off both the first and second placement.
 Place three obituaries and the third placement will be free of charge.
 Each photo published is $125 per day. For example: 2 photos in the paper on 2 days would be 4 photo charges at $500.
Deadlines:
Please follow deadline times to ensure your obituary is published on the day requested.

MEMORIAM (NON-OBITUARY) REQUEST
Unlike an obituary, Memoriam submissions are remembrances of a loved one who has passed. The rates for a memoriam differ from obituaries.
Please call or email us for more memoriam information
Please call 651-228-5280 for more information.
HOURS: Monday – Friday 8:00AM – 5:00PM (CLOSED WEEKENDS and HOLIDAYS)
Please submit your memoriam ad to memoriams@pioneerpress.com or call 651-228-5280.

 By Charles J. DiVencenzo Jr. PUBLISHED: October 25, 2026 at 8:36 AM CDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... On a cold night in late October, the moon rises over the stripped floodplain at Crosby Farm, along the Mississippi in St. Paul, heavy, amber, and uncannily bright.
 Folklore gives this moon a practical name: the Hunter’s Moon. It follows the Harvest Moon, which gave farmers additional evening light to gather the final yield from their fields. By the time the Hunter’s Moon arrived, much of that work was finished. The crops had been cut down to stubble. The thick cover of summer was disappearing. Game became easier to see across the newly exposed ground, making it a moon for noticing what summer had kept hidden.
 By late October, the landscape has lost many of its soft excuses. The corn is gone. The canopy has thinned. Leaves collect in gutters and along curbs, and the contours of the earth emerge again. The season offers less cover now, which may be why its light feels so intimate, arriving just as we begin turning toward the interior of our lives for the long winter ahead.
 We talk a great deal about self-reflection, although much of what passes for reflection is actually surveillance of other people. We inspect the motives of strangers, public figures, and those who have disappointed us with prosecutorial confidence, while the evidence against ourselves tends to get filed elsewhere.
 The harsher discipline is to step into the cold and ask what the stripped field reveals about us.
 A few miles downriver, the burial mounds at Wic̣aḣapi, formerly Indian Mounds Regional Park, hold their place on the bluff above the same water. They have been there for more than 2,000 years, long before any of us arrived with our smaller inventories. Whatever we’re sorting through this month, we’re not the first, and the river has never once rushed anyone through it.
 Some of what we carry is simple enough: old affections, gratitude for good seasons, the quiet weight of people who shaped part of a life before their own lives took them elsewhere. Grief rides along with some of it, a companion for some people and a shield for others. Almost everyone is carrying something that never got a proper ending, and getting older teaches you to stop filing that under failure. An unfinished chapter is just unfinished.
 Two people can build something genuine together and still find themselves living separate lives. They may have created their own language out of music, laughter, and ordinary rituals, then discovered later that the language survived after the conversation ended. What came before stays true, resolved or not. Sometimes the most honest response to a long history is quiet, enduring respect.
 The loons’ calls disappeared from the lakes weeks ago, and the water has seemed quieter since. Under the Hunter’s Moon, when the summer cover is gone, the mind may still wander toward people who have gone silent and places no longer open to us.
 We are tempted to supply the missing explanation. Perhaps there was a misunderstanding. Perhaps the right words would reopen the conversation. Eventually, though, we have to let another person’s silence belong to them. We do not know everything it contains, and grace may require leaving that unreadable portion unread.
 None of that makes the feeling on our side any less real. We can remember someone, care about what happens to them, occasionally wish they were present to see something beautiful, without it becoming a claim on their life. That kind of remembering asks only that we recognize what is ours to carry, what belongs to someone else, and leave the rest of the room open for whoever is actually standing in it.
 Much of what blooms in April was put into the ground in the dark of October. Under the Hunter’s Moon, endings and beginnings occupy the same ground, and some of what it lights is already being planted.
 Soon the tables will be set for Thanksgiving, followed by all the familiar rituals of December. Children grow into adults, and the passing years give family life an entirely new measure of time. Friends gather, siblings repeat old stories, and the people who share our days bring their noise, troubles, and unexpected joy into the room. The old griefs and unanswered questions have to make space for them, or we risk listening so hard for an echo from another season that we miss the conversation already underway.
 The Hunter’s Moon offers a sharp light. Across the harvested fields, it reveals edges and distances, the things that have disappeared and whatever remains standing. It shows you where you’re standing and leaves the verdict to you.
 As the moon climbs and the temperature falls, it catches the State Capitol’s dome above St. Paul, then finds the windows below it until the city is lit against the dark. The ground is bare, but not empty. Somewhere beneath it, April has already begun.
 Charles J. DiVencenzo Jr. is a lawyer and essayist; he lives in Minneapolis.
